translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil, that "God is not the cause of evils"
Many are the forms of teaching that have been given to us by David the psalmist, through the grace of the Holy Spirit who spoke through him.
For at times the prophet tells us of his own sufferings, and how he bravely endured the afflictions that came upon him, and by his own example leaves us a lesson in patience, when he says:
"Lord, why are those who afflict me multiplied?" And again, at times he shows us the goodness of God and the swiftness of his help,
which he gives to those who truly seek him, when he says: "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me."
For he spoke in a manner like that prophet who says: "While you are still speaking, he will say: Behold, here I am."
That is to say: my prayer is not yet finished, and God's hearing has already received its fulfillment.
Again, when he offers prayer to God, he teaches us in what manner we ought to entreat God for our sins, saying:
"Lord, do not reprove me in your anger, nor instruct me in your wrath."
And in the twelfth psalm he reveals the extremity of trials, for he says: "How long, Lord, will you forget me utterly?"
And throughout that whole psalm he has taught us not to be despondent in afflictions, but to wait for the goodness of God and to know
that it is by some good providence that he gives us over to afflictions, and that he brings torments too according to the measure of each person's faith.
Having completed this psalm: "How long, Lord, will you forget me utterly? How long will you turn your face away from me?"
he immediately turned to speak of the wickedness of the godless, who, when some small thing they do not want comes upon them,
they do not bear the coming of afflictions, and they become [?] with doubting minds, and they say:
"Is there a God who takes care of this whole world? Or does he watch over each one, and does he give to each according to what he deserves?"
Then, when they see themselves lingering in those afflictions and trials,
they confirm that evil thought within themselves and decide in their hearts that there is no God, for:
"The fool said in his heart: There is no God." And then, whoever has set this in his heart thereafter engages in every sin without restraint.
For if there is no one who sees all this, and no one who repays each person according to his deeds, what is there to hinder
oppressing the poor? Killing the orphan? Crushing the widow and the stranger?
Entering upon every lawless deed through those impure and defiled passions, and being defiled by all bestial desires?
For this reason he went on to say what goes with the denial of God's existence:
"They have become corrupt and abominable in their lawlessness." For it is impossible to turn aside from the right way unless forgetfulness of God first comes into the heart.
From where is it that the pagans have been given over to that ignorant mind and practice lawlessness?
Is it not from this, that they said, "There is no God"? From where did they fall into those passions of defilement?
And why did their women exchange natural acts for what is against nature, while the men commit shameful acts with men?
Is it not from this, that they exchanged the glory of the one incorruptible God for the likeness of beasts and four-footed creatures and reptiles?
Truly, then, whoever says, "There is no God," is senseless and bereft of understanding and wisdom.
And like him, and in no way behind him in folly, is the one who says, "God is the cause of evils."
For I declare the sin of this one to be equal to that of the first, since both deny his goodness.
The one says, "He does not exist at all," and the other says, "He is not good."
For if he is the cause of evils, he is not good; and for this reason it is evident that both of these alike deny God.
Now people of this kind say: "Then where do illnesses come from? Or where do those untimely deaths come from?
Where do the destructions of cities come from? Shipwrecks? Wars? Slaughters?
For all these are evils, and all of them are the work of God. So whom else shall we take as the cause of all this, if not God?"
Come then, you who say this, since we have fallen into this much-debated inquiry;
let us make a clear beginning to this discourse of ours, and promptly take up this question, and strive to treat its account clearly and without confusion.
First, then, we must hold this firmly in our minds:
that we are creatures of the good God, and our life is from him, and he governs both the small and the great that comes upon us.
And nothing comes upon us apart from his will except sin, for that is from ourselves;
nor is what comes upon us from him in any way evil, as though there were something better than it that anyone could so much as conceive in the mind.
For deaths are from God, yet death is not evil, unless one speaks of the death of the sinner,
for his departure from here becomes the beginning of the torments of hell.
And again, the evils of hell have as their cause not God but we ourselves,
for the beginning and root of sin is our will and free self-determination. For those who were able to keep away from evil and not enter into affliction, such people,
since they fell into sin through desire, what other true word shall we speak, except that they themselves became the cause of torments for themselves?
For evil is of two kinds: the one appears evil to us, while the other is evil by its very nature.
And that evil by nature is done by us: injustice, defilement, folly, cowardice, murders, envy, sorceries,
schemes, and the other passions like these, which defile the soul created in the image of God and darken its beauty.
Again, we call evil whatever is grievous to us and hard to look upon, that is:
sickness of the body, and wounds of the body, and lack of necessary things, and dishonor, and loss of wealth,
and the deaths of one's own kin, each of which comes upon us from the wise and good King for what is better.
For he takes wealth away from those who use it wickedly, so as to make the instrument of their injustice disappear.
And he brings sickness upon those for whom it is better that their limbs be bound and that they be held back from sin.
And death, again, comes when the limits of life are completed,
which the just judgment of God, which sees from of old what is better for each person, established for each one from the very beginning.
Plagues and droughts, or excessive rains, are common afflictions of cities and nations, to punish the excess of their wickedness.
So then, just as a beneficent physician, even if he brings [?] pains or wounds upon the body, is fighting the disease, not the sick person,
so too the good God inflicts these small punishments for the salvation of all.
And you do not blame the physician, who cauterizes one limb, and cuts another, and removes another limb from the body entirely,
but you even pay him a fee and call him savior, because with a small hardship, by cutting off one limb, he stops the pain before the disease has spread through the whole body.
But when you see a city fallen upon those who live in it, or a ship sunk in the sea with its men, you do not hesitate to stir up a blaspheming tongue against the true physician and savior.
Rather, you ought to understand that when people are sick in a mild and easily curable way,
then he strives by his means to heal them, but when the affliction proves to be beyond healing, then it is good to separate what is useless completely from the others,
so that the disease may not advance further, step by step, and reach the vital places.
And just as the cause of cutting or burning is not the physician but the disease,
so too the cause of the destruction of cities is the excess of sin, and God remains far from all blame.
Yet the one who thinks evil says again: "If God is not the cause of evils, how is it said:
'I am the one who created light and made darkness, who make peace and create evil'?
And again it is said: 'Evil came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem,' and:
'There is no evil in a city that the Lord has not done,' and in the great song of Moses it is said:
'See, see, that I am, and there is no God besides me. I put to death and I give life, I wound and I heal.'"
But in not one of these sayings, for anyone who has a mind and understands, is any accusation of God to be found, that he is the cause and doer of evil.
For he who said, "I created light and made darkness," shows himself to be the creator of all created things, and not a doer of evil,
so that you should not say that one is the maker of day and light and another the maker of night.
For this reason he declared himself the creator of all this, of everything created, even though these things appear opposed to one another,
so that you should not seek one creator of fire and another of water, nor one maker of air and another of earth,
for they appear by nature to be opposed to one another, and some have stumbled over this and fallen into polytheism.
But he makes peace and creates evil: for he makes peace within you,
when through good teaching he makes peace in your mind and subjects to the spirit the desires of the flesh, which are opposed to it.
And he creates evil: it does not say, "I create an evil deed," but rather he creates the evil man, that is to say,
that he changes it and brings it into another form, so that it may abandon wickedness and take on the nature of the good. For he says:

"Create a pure heart in me, O God." He does not mean, "Now make another heart out of nothing," but rather, "Renew this heart that has grown old through wickedness and evil deeds." And again it is said:
"That he might create the two together into one new man." Here "create" does not mean making out of nothing, but changing for the good those who already exist.
And again it says, "Whoever is in Christ is a new creation." And again Moses the prophet says:
"Was it not this very Father of yours who acquired you, and made you, and created you?"
For see, here the word "creation" is plainly placed after "making," and it teaches us
that this word "creation" is used in many places of renewal and of changing for the better.
Now understand, then, that when he makes peace, he makes peace in this way, by creating evil people, that is, by changing them and bringing them to something better.
And again, if you understand peace as the cessation of wars, and call evil those hardships
which follow wars, namely military campaigns in distant lands, pains, sleepless nights, sweat, wounds, deaths, the plundering of cities,
the enslavement of people, the pitiable experiences of captives, and all the other evils that follow wars, we say
that they come about by the just judgment of God, who through wars brings punishments upon those who deserve punishment.
Or would you wish that Sodom had not been burned after such great evils of theirs?
Or that Jerusalem had not fallen and the temple had not been laid waste after that terrible sin of the Jews against the Lord?
And how else was it right for such things to be done, if not by the hand of the Romans, to whom the Jews, those enemies of their own life, handed over our Lord?
It is clear, then, that the evils of wars come justly upon those who deserve them. And again, the saying:
"I kill and I make alive": if you wish, accept it in its plain sense,
For fear restrains those simple souls: "I will wound and I will heal" — and this too is good,
if you understand it in this way, according to its plain meaning: that the wounding brings fear and the healing leads to love.
but it is fitting for you to understand it in a higher sense:
"I kill from sin," that is, I cut a person off from it completely, "and I make alive by righteousness."
for "though the outer man is being destroyed, the inner is being renewed." And it is not that he kills one person and makes another alive, but rather the same one.
By that with which he kills, by it he makes alive, and by that through which he wounds, by it he heals, in keeping with the proverb that says:
"You struck him with the rod, but you delivered his soul from death."
So then, the flesh is wounded so that the soul may be healed, and one dies to sin so that one may live by righteousness.
And as for "Evil came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem," its meaning is clear.
What evils? That is, the clash of weapons and of horsemen. And again, when you hear:
"There is no evil in the city that the Lord has not done," understand the word "evil" as the punishment
that comes upon sinners for their correction. This is what this saying signifies. For he says:
"I afflicted you and [?] made you a servant," so that I might do you good. Before lawlessness overflows, he holds it back as one holds back a river, with a strong opposing force and a firm barrier.
For this reason there are diseases of cities and of nations, rainless skies, barrenness of the earth, and all the hardships of this world,
which come upon each person and hold back the growth of wickedness.
And such evils as these come about from God, so that through them there may be deliverance from those true evils,
for sicknesses of the body and those other evils serve to hold back sin.
For God does away with evil, but it is not that evil is from God; for a physician too, in order to do away with disease, touches the body.
And again, the devastations of cities, earthquakes and collapses, the destruction of armies, the sinking of ships, and all the ruin of peoples,
whether they come about by earth, or sea, or air, or fire, or by some other cause, happen to frighten and turn back those who remain,
when God quells the wickedness of a whole people through such plagues.
For that true evil, which is sin, which more than anything deserves this name of evil, comes from our own will and intention.
For it is within our power either to separate ourselves from evil or to remain in evil.
But as for those other evils, which are not sin, some of them come about as a test and to reveal courage,
such as came upon Job: the death of his children in a single moment, the sudden loss of all his wealth, and that wounding of his body.
And again, some come about to heal sin, such as came upon David: that shame from his own house, as a punishment for his evil desire.
And again, thirdly, there is yet another kind of torment, which comes from the just judgment of God to frighten those who go easily toward sin,
as Dathan and Abiram were swallowed up by the earth, when the abyss opened its mouth over them.
For here it is not that they themselves became any better from that punishment; for how could those who went down to hell become better?
But the others who remained were frightened by the example of their fate and turned back. In this way Pharaoh was drowned together with his warriors,
and in this way those who formerly dwelt in Palestine perished. And although the apostle says:
"vessels of wrath, made for destruction," let us not suppose that the created nature of Pharaoh was something evil; for if we say this,
the blame reaches back to the Creator. Rather, when you hear "vessel," understand that each of us has been created for some use.
And as in a great house some vessels are of gold and some of silver and some of clay and some of wood, for the mind of each person takes on the likeness of these materials:
the golden vessel is the one who is pure in deed and without guile; and the silver, the one who is inferior to him in worth;
and the clay, the one who thinks earthly things and is easily shattered;
and the wooden, the one who is easily defiled by sin and becomes fuel for the eternal fire. So also a vessel of wrath is
one who has received and held every work of the devil, as a vessel does, and because of the stench
that he has taken on from that corruption can no longer be fit for use, but is worthy only of being done away with and destroyed.
Therefore, since the wise steward of souls knew that his shattering was necessary, he so arranged matters
that he should become famous and renowned among all, so that when he was shattered his suffering might be of benefit to others,
since he was incurable because of his great wickedness. So he hardened him by long-suffering and by that delay of punishment, so that in this way his evil might increase.
And when his wickedness had grown to the final limit, then the justice of the divine judgment would be shown forth upon him.
For this reason he began with small punishments and increased them from time to time.
And he could not bend his hardness, but found that he despised even the power of God, and to the afflictions too
that came upon him he grew accustomed; and even so he did not give him over to death, until he himself drowned himself through his own pride,
when he dared to pass along the way of the righteous and supposed that, as for the people of God, so for him too the Red Sea would become passable.
Behold then, you know all this from God, and you hold distinct in your mind the kinds of evil, and you know what the true evil is, namely sin,
whose end is destruction; and what the supposed evil is, painful to look upon yet having the power of good,
such as afflictions that come to restrain sin, whose fruit is the eternal life of souls.
And since you know all this, cease from this conduct of yours, in which the dispensations of God do not please you, and by no means count God as the cause of evil,
nor again suppose that evil has any substance of its own.
For wickedness is not a substance, like some living creature, nor is any nature of it found to have come into being anywhere; rather, evil is a deficiency of good.
For the eye was created, but blindness comes from the loss of the eyes.
Now, if the eye were not of a corruptible nature, blindness would find no place, for it does not have substance.
Likewise, evil does not have a substance of its own, but comes about through the blinding of the soul.
For neither is it uncreated, as the lawless claim in their teaching, who make evil equal to the good and excellent nature.
For if both are without beginning and above creation, then surely they are equal.
Nor again is it created, for if all created things are from God, how could evil be from the good?
For neither is defilement from holiness, nor wickedness from virtue.
Read "the creation of the world" and you will find that there "everything is good and very good."
So evil was not created along with good things; and neither were those invisible created beings created by God mixed with evil.
For if evil was not created along with these bodily things, how could it have been created along with the bodiless beings, who so far surpass them in purity?
But those who talk about evil say:
"Look, evil exists, and its work shows that it exists, for it is spread over the whole of our life."
Where then does its substance come from, if it is neither without beginning and uncreated, nor created?"
But I will ask those who say such things: Where does disease come from? Where do blindnesses of the eyes come from?

For disease is not uncreated, nor is it created by God, and no one can say this; rather, living creatures were created in a fitting creation according to nature and received life with completeness of limbs.
But they become sick when they turn aside from what is natural, for they depart from health either through disorderly harmful foods or through some other cause
that leads to sickness. For it is evident that God created bodies, but not disease;
and he created the soul, but not sin; rather, the soul became evil when it turned aside from what is natural. And what was that first good of its own?
Contemplation by the providence of God and union with him through love; and when it fell from this, it was seized by those many and various evils.
Again, on this point those improper people say: "And why was it created at all as capable of receiving evil?"
And they do not understand that it was made so for the sake of free will, which above all befits a rational nature,

for man received from the Creator a life released from all compulsion and self-governing, because he was created as the image of God; and he understands the good and knows how to receive it, and he has the authority and the power
to remain in the contemplation of the good and the discipline of intelligible things, and so to preserve that natural life of his.
And again, he has the authority, if he wishes, to turn away from the good. And this comes upon him

when he takes his fill of that blessed rest and joy, and grows heavy as if with sleep, and comes down from those lofty things into lowliness, and for the sake of defiled pleasures mingles with the flesh.
Adam was once in heaven, not in place but in mind. When he had been given a soul and looked up to heaven, and rejoiced at the things he saw,
he loved all the more the Benefactor, who had granted him the delight of eternal life, had given him rest among the good things of paradise, and had given him dominion,
made him like the angels, made him a companion of the archangels, and made him a hearer of the divine voice.
Being established by God in all this and taking delight in it, he soon became sated with it all.

And through that satiety, as if he held it in contempt, he honored the beauty visible to the eyes of the flesh above the beauty perceived by the mind, and he chose the fullness of the belly over those enduring good things.
And immediately he was outside paradise and outside that blessed life, and he became evil not by compulsion but voluntarily.
Therefore he sinned because of his evil will, and he died because of sin, for:
"Death belongs to sin." For the farther he withdrew from life, the nearer he came to death, since God is life,
And separation from life is death. It is clear, then, that Adam brought death upon himself by his own choice, through separating himself from God, as it is written:
"Behold, those who have removed themselves from you shall perish."
And so it was not God who created death, but we who brought it upon ourselves through the wickedness of our wills and intentions.
Yet for the reasons stated earlier, God did not prevent that dissolution either, so that he might not make that sickness immortal in us,
just as a potter does not consent to commit a cracked clay vessel to the fire until he has broken it up and, by forming it a second time, healed the damage it had.
But on this point the inquirer speaks again: "And why was sinlessness not given to us at our very creation, so that even if we wished to, we would be unable to sin?"
But listen, you who say this: you too do not regard your servant as faithful when you keep him bound, but when you see that he does your will voluntarily.
And God too does not love what is coerced and compelled, but the person who advances by virtue.
But virtue is practiced voluntarily and not by compulsion, and the will lies with us, and that which lies with us is self-determination.
So whoever blames the Creator, asking why he did not create us sinless by compulsion, does nothing other than
honor the nature of irrational animals above rational nature, and what is unmoved and without will above what is voluntary and active.
All this [?] has been well said, so that you may not fall into the abyss of inquiry, failing to find what you seek and along with it being cast out from God as well.
Let us cease, then, from instructing the All-wise One; let us cease from seeking something better than his works,
for although the reasons and causes of each of his dispensations are unknown to us,
yet let us establish this one teaching in our souls: that nothing evil comes from the Good One.
But again, following upon all this, there comes in turn the inquiry about the devil: where does the devil come from, if evils are not from God?
But what shall we say? We say this: that on this matter too the same word suffices for us that we spoke concerning the wickedness of human beings, for:
From where did man become evil? From his own will. And from where does the devil's wickedness come?
From the same cause, for he too had a life of free will, and it was in his power either to be with God or to become estranged from the Good One.
For Gabriel is an angel and stands always before God, and Satan too was an angel, and he fell utterly from his honor.
The one his good will preserved in the heavens, and the other that same self-governing will cast down from heaven.
For the one could also have rebelled had he wished, and the other could also have not fallen.
But the one was made firm by his insatiable love of God, while the other was cast away by separation from God.
This is that evil: estrangement from God. For a small turning of the eye places us either with the sun or with our own shadow:
when we look up there, the light is ready to illumine us, and when we look down at the shadow, we no longer see the light.
In this way the devil became evil, for he took on evil willingly, and it was not that his nature was opposed to the good.
From where, then, comes his implacable war against us?
For since he became receptive of every evil, he also took on the disease of envy and envied us our honor.
For he could not bear our untroubled life in paradise, but with guile he deceived man by a stratagem, and man's desire,
which he had for likeness to God, he used as a means of temptation, and he showed him the tree and promised, through eating
of it, that they would become gods, for he said: "If you eat, you will be like gods, knowing good and evil."
He was not, however, created as our enemy, but became our enemy through envy,
for he saw himself fallen from among the angels and could not bear to see the one made from earth rising to the honor of the angels by advancing in exaltation.
Since, then, he became an enemy, from that time God established among us enmity toward him. For this reason, to that beast which served him
God spoke, and directed his wrath toward him, saying: "I will put enmity between you and his seed."
For truly, peace with the wicked one is harmful, for this law of friendship is seen among those joined by likeness,
and therefore it is well said: "Evil conversations corrupt good morals."
For just as in those sultry lands the air, entering little by little through the breathing passages, imperceptibly brings disease upon those who live there,
so too the habit of loving the wicked leaves a great evil in the soul, even if at the time the harm goes unnoticed.
For this reason, then, implacable enmity has been given to us toward the serpent. And if the instrument is so worthy of hatred, how much more ought the one who acted through it to be hated?
But some say: "And why was that tree in paradise, through which the devil's assault on us came about?
For if it had not held that occasion of disobedience, how would we have been cast down to death through disobedience?"
But understand that it was necessary for a commandment to be given that would test our obedience; for this reason there was the tree, bearing beautiful fruits,
so that by abstaining from desire we might show forth the good of fasting, and thus justly become worthy of the crowns of patience.
Now the eating was followed not only by disobedience to the commandment but also by the knowledge of nakedness, for it says:
"They ate, and their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked." But it was proper that this nakedness should remain unknown,

so that man should not be anxious to make up for that deficiency by procuring clothing as a comfort for his nakedness, and through this care for the flesh be corrupted and drawn away from gazing upon God.
So they say: "And why was clothing not created on him immediately?"
But hear that this was neither proper nor fitting, that he should have clothing either from nature or made by art.
For natural coverings befit the beasts: feathers and hair and thickness of hide, for enduring winter and bearing heat,
and among them none has any advantage over another, but their nature is equal in honor.
But it was fitting for man that, in proportion to his love for God, he should also have distinct gifts of good things.
For this reason it was not proper for him to have clothing by nature. And again, if it had been given to him from the beginning to procure it by art,
this too would have brought about lack of leisure, which above all man was to flee as something harmful.
For this reason too the Lord calls us back to the life of paradise itself and drives care out of our souls, saying: "Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will put on."
So clothing was not to be given to him either by nature or by art, but other garments had been prepared for him, if he had kept to virtue,
that is, garments made by the grace of God, which were to shine forth upon man, garments of light, such as those of the angels are:
more beautiful than the loveliness of flowers, more radiant and pure than the beauty of the stars.

For this reason garments were not given to man immediately when he was created, for they were being kept for him as rewards of virtue and were to be given at that later time, which he did not reach because of that temptation of the devil.
Now then, since our fall has taken place, the devil is our adversary, for the Lord has ordained our battle against him,
so that through this obedience we may reverse that victory, overcome him, and be crowned by victory over him.
For would that he had not become a devil, but had remained in the rank in which he was appointed from the beginning by the Creator.
But since he became an apostate, he showed himself an enemy of God and an enemy of men, who were created in the image of God; for this reason he is a hater of mankind,
because he is a fighter against God, and he hates us as creatures of God, and again he hates us
as made in the likeness of God. But he who wisely governs all things, and with foreknowledge, made use of his wickedness for the testing of our souls,
Just as a physician uses the venom of a viper as a medicine. Some people, then, ask us:
"And what is the devil? And what is his rank? And what is his dignity? And why was he given the name Satan?"
He was called Satan, then, because he is the opponent of what is good, for this is what the language of the Hebrews signifies:
that Satan means opponent. As we find in the book of Kings: "God raised up against Solomon a satan, Hadad, king of the Syrians."
And he is given the name devil because he is an accuser, for "devil" is translated as "accuser,"
since he becomes our helper toward sin, and then he himself becomes our accuser; he rejoices over our destruction and then exposes our deeds.
His nature is bodiless, according to the word of the apostle, who says:
"Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against evil spirits." And his rank is principality, for he says:
"Against the principalities and the powers, the world-rulers of darkness." And the place of his principality is the air.
For the same apostle says: "According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience."
For this reason he is also called the ruler of the world, for his rule is over the earth. And thus the Lord says:
"Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out," and again he says: "The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me."
Since, then, it has been said concerning the army of the devil:
"The evil spirits are under heaven": it should be understood that Scripture customarily gives the name [of heaven] to the air, as when it says:
"They go up to the heavens." And: "The birds of heaven." For when it was said, "They go up to the heavens," this means that they go up to the height.
For this reason Christ also saw the devil as lightning falling down, that is, fallen from his own rule and come down to earth, so that he might be trampled by those who believe in Christ,

for he gave his disciples authority to trample on snakes and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. Since, then, that evil tyranny of his has been cast out and the world has been purified by the passion of the cross,
which made peace between the things of earth and those of heaven, from then on the kingdom of heaven is proclaimed to us. For John said:
"The kingdom of heaven has drawn near," and the Lord preached the gospel of the kingdom in every place; and again, before this, the angels cried out:
"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace," and again, those who rejoiced over the Lord's entry into Jerusalem said:
"Peace in heaven and glory in the highest." And thus there are many songs of victory that signify the complete fall of the enemy,
so that there is no longer any battle or opposition to our ascent to heaven, nor anyone to keep us from that blessed life,

but we have without hardship the inheritance of life, and, after these present times, we are to take from the tree of life forever, from which we were at first barred from taking through the counsel of the serpent.
For "God set the cherubim and the burning, turning sword to guard the way of the tree of life,"
which may we pass through without hindrance and enter within, into those delights of good things, through Christ Jesus,
our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
